options.title: The Doctor Who Was Mocked For Washing His Hands
options.description:
In 1847, Dr. Ignaz Semmelweis discovered that washing hands in chlorine solution dramatically reduced hospital mortality, despite fierce backlash from his peers.

Sources:
- Carter, K. C. (1983). Childbed Fever: A Scientific Biography of Ignaz Semmelweis.
- World Health Organization Historical Archives on Infection Control.
script_lines: In 1847, a Hungarian doctor began scrubbing his hands in bleach solution before delivering babies, and his boss tried to ruin his career for it.
Doctors in Vienna walked straight from dissecting corpses into the delivery room without washing up.
Clinic director Dr. Klein mocked the new routine, calling it "an insulting waste of time that blames gentlemen."
Ignaz Semmelweis stood by his basin and snapped back, "The truth does not care about your dignity."
Staff complained about the harsh chemical smell, but Semmelweis forced every doctor to scrub at the door.
Within weeks, maternity ward mortality plunged from eighteen percent down to under two percent.
Microscopic particles were jumping from cadavers like invisible flour dusted across a table, until chlorine neutralised them.
He revolutionized medicine forever, simply by refusing to stop scrubbing.

options.title: The Doctor Who Studied Digestion Through an Open Hole
options.description:
In 1823, Dr. William Beaumont conducted pioneering experiments on human digestion through a fistulous hole in Alexis St. Martin's stomach.

Sources:
- Beaumont, W. (1833). Experiments and Observations on the Gastric Juice, and the Physiology of Digestion.
- Smithsonian Institution Archives.
script_lines: In 1823, an army surgeon began dangling raw meat on silk strings directly into a living man's stomach hole.
Patient Alexis St. Martin had survived an accident that left a permanent open flap in his abdomen.
Local doctors mocked the experiment, calling it "a grotesque circus stunt that proves nothing."
Dr. William Beaumont ignored them and muttered, "I am watching human digestion happen in real time."
Alexis endured months of raw beef and cabbage being inserted and pulled out every hour.
Beaumont collected clear gastric juice and showed that stomach acid chemically dissolved the food.
Hydrochloric acid breaks down protein like battery acid melting copper, operating on precise multi-hour cycles.
Modern digestive science was born, all because one doctor refused to close an open door.

options.title: The Cage That Stopped Fire Underground
options.description:
In 1815, Sir Humphry Davy invented the miner's safety lamp, preventing explosive coal mine gas ignitions using fine wire mesh.

Sources:
- Davy, H. (1818). On the Safety Lamp for Coal Mines.
- Science Museum Group Collection.
script_lines: In 1815, an inventor carried a glowing open flame straight into a chamber of explosive gas to prove wire mesh could stop a bomb.
Coal mines across Britain were constantly exploding whenever tallow candles hit trapped methane pockets underground.
Mine engineers laughed at his design, calling a metal grid "a useless cage that cannot block real fire."
Sir Humphry Davy lowered his lantern inside and insisted, "Metal steals heat faster than gas can catch."
Miners watched nervously as flammable gas filled the chamber surrounding the burning wick.
The blue methane flame flared inside the gauze, but the air outside never ignited.
Fine copper mesh absorbs thermal energy like a metal radiator, keeping gas below its six-hundred-degree ignition point.
Coal miners went to work carrying bare flames, saved by a simple metal screen.
